tagline: Down Kaaterskill Clove, two thousand feet in two miles.
intro: From Hunter village, Route 23A climbs east under Hunter Mountain, past the head of Stony Clove Notch with the Devil's Path range in full view to the south, and through Tannersville to a crest of 2,300 feet. Then it drops 2,000 feet in two miles down Kaaterskill Clove to Palenville, the view that inspired many Hudson River School paintings.

The side roads have their own stories. Route 214 runs south through Stony Clove Notch on a tannery road opened by 1849 for hauling hemlock bark, and Platte Clove Road climbs the north wall of the escarpment's other break, a grade where some of the world's best bicycle racers once got off and walked.

moments.title: Tannersville
moments.text: A tannery village turned summer resort, whose downtown buildings have been painted in multicolored pastels with cartoon pictures on the shutters.

moments.title: Kaaterskill Falls
moments.text: Thomas Cole first came in 1825 and painted these two cascades, 260 feet in all, and walkers from the trailhead must use the narrow shoulder of 23A for a good way to reach them.

moments.title: Palenville
moments.text: The hamlet at the foot of the clove was the fictional home of Rip Van Winkle, and has been called the first art colony in America.

practical: Platte Clove Road is gated shut and left unplowed each winter, usually from November until late April or early May, depending on weather and repairs.
